There is a slight disconnect here with reality, it would seem. Essentially, there is the assumption that the whole world freezes in time unless there is a post. It would be more reasonable for us to assume that everything has simply gone in the same direction as it was going. Things change, if they were clearly going to change.

We do this already with GDP and population calculations. We look at trends and apply them to the years in between the start of the game and claiming. It's not so far-fetched to look at trends for other aspects.

If the trend in Colombia from 2010-2015 is that the drug trade is lessening, wouldn't it be safe to assume that trend continues past 2015? Why should we treat it as if that progress suddenly stopped? It makes no sense to claim that in-game inaction changes real life trends. If anything, no change in the current progress would mean that it progresses as it has been doing.

Liberia has had arms/military embargoes against it since 1992. Those embargoes are temporary- they expire and are reevaluated. During the time of the civil wars, this reevaluation has meant the embargoes are renewed. Between 2003 and 2015, with peace in Liberia, those embargoes were once again renewed. However, there was a trend- they were becoming less restrictive.

How can we say we must continue one trend (the renewal of the embargoes) and not continue the trend which is intrinsically linked to it (the decline of restrictiveness)? There has been no change in Liberia in that time in regards to peace and war. Liberia was as peaceful as it had been when the embargoes were being relaxed. It thus follows that the trend continues of the embargoes being relaxed.

Yet this is not the case, according to some members of the moderation team. Why should we continue only some trends while abruptly ceasing others? It does not make sense.

I’ve always assumed that things were done via reasonable interpolation (what we use for GDP and population): analysing past and current actions to interpolate rather simple events in the future. For example, if the Chinese were building a Great Wall from 2014-2018, we would expect it done in 2020.

For anything more complex than that, there would have to be obvious proof that the trend would continue. For example statements from economists and scientists on the dropping of the price of graphene would be reason to believe the price would be lower in 2029, rather than assuming that the price stays at its 2015 rate and only begins dropping again at its first mention on /v/ModernPowers, even if this mention is in 2029.

Some things are much harder to substantiate because they rely on the belief that science will inevitably reach certain goals. The Skylon space rocket is an example of this. We know that it is currently being funded and researched in real life, but it’s a very new type of science that is currently in the early stages of its research.
